references.text: Describes the holy anointing oil that was to be made according to the art of anointing, as verse 32 refers to
Parallel command regarding the incense, which was also holy and not to be imitated for private use
Shows the proper use of the anointing oil—to anoint the priest Aaron
Moses anoints Aaron with the holy oil as described in Exodus
Emphasizes the distinction between the holy and the common, which is the core of the prohibition in verse 32
The high priest is anointed with the holy oil and must remain holy
Poetic reference to the precious anointing oil that ran down over Aaron's head and beard
The consequence of breaking the prohibition in verse 32—to be cut off from one's people
Both verses emphasize the principle that holy objects (oil/incense) are strictly limited to their liturgical function and must not be used on ordinary people or in foreign forms.
Both verses link the consecration of persons (priests) to their service with the holy objects (bread/oil), and stress that a holy status is a prerequisite for handling what is holy.
Both verses use identical theological logic: that the holy is reserved for the initiated, and explicitly forbidden for 'strangers' (ordinary people) to touch or enjoy.
Both verses emphasize the principle of exclusivity in God's service: one must make neither 'another' oil nor other gods, but adhere strictly to what God has commanded.
Both verses are based on God's holy nature as the foundation for the requirement of separation: the oil is holy because it belongs to a holy God, just as the people are called to be holy.
